title: An Alternative Theory of Unions
candidate_workflows: When a market is growing rapidly, prioritize expansion and critical deadlines over marginal cost optimization; pay a reasonable premium to remove mundane bottlenecks, then revisit efficiency as growth stabilizes.
Before treating an expensive resource as a durable benchmark, ask whether its price reflects temporary scarcity and the value of speed in a fast-growing market.

title: The Equity Equation
candidate_workflows: For any equity trade of fraction n, require the post-trade average outcome to exceed 1/(1-n) times the pre-trade outcome, equivalently a fractional improvement greater than n/(1-n), then verify that the remaining ownership is worth more than the original whole.
For a proposed hire, estimate the outcome multiplier i and use n=(i-1)/i as a break-even ceiling before subtracting salary, overhead, and a required company margin.
Treat the formula as a way to expose assumptions rather than an automatic answer; record non-financial terms and uncertainty alongside the estimate.

title: Stuff
exclusion_reason: The essay concerns personal ownership of consumer goods, clutter, and household purchasing habits; although it offers a purchase test, it does not connect that test to startup formation, product, users, teams, funding, or a sufficiently specific founder work process.

title: Holding a Program in One's Head
candidate_workflows: At the start of a technical project, reduce the scope to a prototype that one person can mentally model, and allow the implementation to change both the solution and the problem being solved.
Protect long uninterrupted coding blocks, avoid scheduled interruptions, use succinct abstractions, and rewrite until the code is easy for its owner to reload and change.

Keep the group small and partition the system into components with clear individual ownership so integrated redesign remains possible; favor problems where this concentrated judgment beats a large organization.

title: How Not to Die
candidate_workflows: Create a recurring external progress cadence with advisers or peers and report concrete releases, deals, and learning so silence and stagnation become visible early.

Treat severe morale swings and an indifferent first launch as normal; look for a small group of ecstatic users, identify what they love, expand that core, and change the product if no such users exist.
Prevent soft abandonment by removing competing commitments and maintaining public accountability; when setbacks arrive, keep iterating and be willing to change the company without giving up on it.

title: News from the Front
candidate_workflows: In founder or hiring selection, consciously discount school prestige and evaluate the individual through demonstrated ability, direct conversation, projects, and outcomes users can judge.
Calibrate selection heuristics against observed success and failure, and update them when direct evidence repeatedly conflicts with a prestigious brand.
For personal development, optimize for learning, making, and finding capable peers rather than for credentials whose value depends on institutional gatekeeping.

title: How to Do Philosophy
candidate_workflows: When an abstract debate stalls, inspect whether fuzzy words or an incomplete partition are generating the disagreement, then lower the abstraction level or define an operational meaning.
Test a general idea by whether understanding it changes an action; begin with a useful specific observation and increase its generality only while preserving applicability.
Treat revered frameworks as provisional versions to debug and supersede rather than as authorities that can only be interpreted.

title: The Future of Web Startups
candidate_workflows: When startup costs fall, exploit the change by launching a working product cheaply and approaching investors with performance evidence instead of relying on a business plan and presentation skill.
Standardize repeatable, non-differentiating processes and deal terms while releasing a minimal product quickly and letting user needs guide what changes.

Treat acquisition as a normal build-versus-buy option rather than evidence of internal inadequacy; standardize the process, use later-stage performance evidence to select targets, and unite technically informed discovery with deal execution to reduce friction and make delayed purchases accountable.

Set risk strategy according to exposure: investors can favor risky bets because a portfolio averages outcomes, while founders with one concentrated company may rationally be more conservative; apply portfolio-style risk only when lower startup costs give founders multiple independent attempts.

Evaluate a startup hub by its marginal advantage over competitors and its effect on success, not by whether the company can technically start elsewhere; include mobility and face-to-face network effects in the comparison.
Expect lower startup costs to increase competitors, so act on good ideas sooner and use direct performance rather than credentials or institutional approval as the selection test.

title: Why to Move to a Startup Hub
candidate_workflows: Choose a location by comparing the specialized knowledge, investor market, face-to-face access, and competitor advantage each place provides, rather than asking whether a move is strictly necessary.

Make the relocation decision conditional on family disruption, immigration cost, industry-specific centers, and a definite funding offer; reject moves whose attention cost exceeds the network benefit.
Distinguish a firm funding commitment from investor interest, and assess a hub's investors by informed boldness and speed rather than by a reputation for prudence.

title: Six Principles for Making New Things
candidate_workflows: Find an overlooked problem that genuinely needs solving, identify the simplest solution, and separate the real user need from difficult or impressive work that does not matter.
Deliver the smallest crude version informally as soon as possible, learn from users, and iterate rapidly instead of polishing an internally imagined final design.
Treat contempt caused by a solution looking small, incomplete, or unconventional as weak negative evidence; judge whether it solves the real problem and benefits from low competition.

title: Trolls
candidate_workflows: Diagnose abusive community behavior through social distance, participants' communication skill, and the conduct the forum visibly tolerates.
Set a face-to-face behavioral standard, recruit members to reinforce it, remove deliberate trolls promptly, and expose peer reputation feedback where it changes low-investment behavior.
Intervene before thoughtful users leave and abusive behavior becomes the default culture; test whether moderation suppresses substantive dissent or mainly discourages disposable insults.

title: A New Venture Animal
candidate_workflows: For capital-light software and web startups, match the ratio of hands-on help to capital to the company's stage: at the earliest stage founder living costs may dominate, so little money and intensive help can resolve fundamental uncertainty; do not generalize this model to biotech or other expensive categories that remain capital-heavy.
Before launching a company, clear cofounder tensions, legal setup, focus ambiguity, immediate obstacles, and distractions; protect building time and create a concrete deadline for investor exposure.
Separate company launch from product launch and judge readiness by the next financing and execution milestone when the product cannot yet ship.
Use what the company is making to bound downstream decisions about hiring, fundraising, and marketing.

title: You Weren't Meant to Have a Boss
candidate_workflows: For maker work, compare roles by how much they permit building, initiative, and learning through doing rather than by immediate salary, brand, or apparent safety.
Keep a technology organization as small as each stage allows and hire exceptional people because mediocre hires reduce output while adding the coordination cost of extra headcount.
When scale is necessary, preserve initiative through genuinely independent groups or components; for an individual seeking maximum autonomy, prefer founding or joining very early.

title: How to Disagree
candidate_workflows: Classify a disagreement by what it addresses and move responses away from the person, authority, or tone toward a counterargument supported by reasoning and evidence.
State the other side's central point, quote the exact claim or dependency you dispute, and explain the error; if addressing a different issue, say so explicitly.
Use the disagreement level as an upper bound on persuasiveness rather than a truth score, and remove meanness that distracts from a substantive case.

title: Some Heroes
candidate_workflows: Choose operational role models by asking whether their behavior would guide a decision in the same situation, then extract recurring standards such as deep care for the work and refusal to pander.
Calibrate every claim to its confidence with precise qualification, and treat accuracy about how certain you are as part of being correct.
Counter the immediate rewards of small tasks by deliberately seeking consequential questions that others have not yet recognized as questions.

title: Why There Aren't More Googles
candidate_workflows: Treat an acquisition offer as a valuation and option decision rather than a test of mission; model the independent upside before accepting, and as a buyer reconsider increasing an offer a strong startup rejects.

Evaluate novel startups independently of investor consensus, expect the strongest ideas to look risky, and diagnose whether check size, career risk, or lack of technical understanding is driving conservatism.
Adapt check size, diligence, and governance to cheaper startups by making more small bets, requiring less certainty, and avoiding board overhead that is disproportionate to the investment.

title: Be Good
candidate_workflows: In the early phase, prioritize making something people want over premature business-model optimization while still checking that the beneficiaries or resulting growth can eventually support the company.
When morale falls, anchor the team on users who need the product; launch quickly, care for those users, and turn their needs into the next product decision.
Use doing what is best for users as a default decision rule, and make the investor case through genuine user love, referrals, and organic growth rather than salesmanship alone.
Use benevolence as a stateless rule that scales across fast decisions, but hold good intentions accountable to actual effects.

title: Lies We Tell Kids
candidate_workflows: Audit beliefs learned for protection, social peace, identity, authority, or group management, and separate their factual content from the incentives that made the simplified story convenient.
Treat institutional rules as possible hacks for managing large groups rather than universal laws of success, and retest them against direct evidence in the current environment.
Use contradictions and access to behind-the-scenes incentives to identify misleading priors, then consciously remove them instead of assuming you begin from a neutral position.

title: Disconnecting Distraction
candidate_workflows: Map distractions that masquerade as work or appear during transitions between projects, and track intermittent losses instead of judging only periods of deep engagement.
Treat distraction as an evolving adversary and replace intention-only rules with visible friction or alarms that make every lapse deliberate.

Validate any environmental control over time and revise it when avoidance returns; the essay's separate-computer implementation later failed, so retain the visibility principle rather than copying that setup as proven.
